heading: 4 Justification of Self and of Nation
title_zh: 第四章　為己辯護，也為國辯護
src: While Uchimura had worked on the two books that described the difficulties of the Christian life in Japan, he had also been writing two works in English that he intended for a Western audience. He finished the first, How I Became a Christian, in November 1893. The second, Japan and the Japanese, he did not finish until September 1894, after war broke out with China and Japan’s successes began to attract the attention of an admiring Western public.

How I Became a Christian pleads that Christians in the West should sympathize with the tremendous upheaval that conversion to Christianity occasions in the soul of the convert. Its 53,000 words impress a reader as frank autobiography. The subtitle, Out of My Diary, heightens this impression. In form, the book consists of what seem to be direct quotations from a diary complete with dates; to these entries are added explanations about them and essays on subjects occasioned by them. How I Became a Christian forms one of the principal sources of this work from Uchimura’s birth until his return from the United States – his family background and childhood; conversion; the student church in Sapporo; the restless year in Tokyo; the arrival in the United States; work in a hospital for feeble-minded children; life in Amherst and in a theological seminary; and his impressions of “Christendom” upon return home.

Numerous passages within the essays employ a style that impresses the reader with the sincerity of the author and almost compels one to empathize with him. One paragraph describes his disillusion when Kanzô arrives in the United States to find it not the paradise that he had been led to expect: “O heaven, I am undone! I was deceived! I gave up what was really Peace for that which is no Peace! To go back to my old faith I am now too overgrown; to acquiesce in my new faith is impossible. O for Blessed Ignorance that might have kept me from the knowledge of faith other than that which satisfied my good Grandma! It made her industrious, patient, true; and not a compunction clouded her face as she drew her last breath. Hers was Peace and mine is Doubt.”
If some passages plead for pity, others cut with unexpected satire. Uchimura portrays, for instance, his shocked first encounter with the profanity endemic in a Christian nation:

> Yes, Hebraism in one sense at least, I found to be a common form of speech in America. First of all, everybody has a Christian name, and even horses are christened there. In a hotel-parlor we asked a respectable-looking gentleman how he liked the new president-elect (Cleveland), and his emphatic answer was strongly Hebraic. “By G--,” he said, “I tell you he is a devil.” We started in an emigrant train toward the east, and when the car stopped with a jerk so that we were almost thrown out of our seats, one of our fellow passengers expressed his vexation with another Hebraism, “J---- C-----.”

Later Uchimura shows both how he understood the racial prejudice then prevalent on the East Coast and how it hurt to have every Oriental considered a “Chinese,” by which term, as then used, Americans meant almost exclusively day labourers and menials:

> A group of young Japanese engineers went to examine the Brooklyn Bridge. When under the pier, the structure and tension of each of the suspending ropes were being discussed upon, a silk-hatted, bespectacled, and decently dressed American gentleman approached them. “Well John,” he intruded upon the Japanese scientists, “these things must look awful strange to you from China, ey!” One among the Japanese retorted the insulting question, and said, “so they must be to you from Ireland.” The gentleman got angry and said, “No, indeed not. I am not an Irish.” “And so we are not Chinese,” was the gentle rejoinder. It was a good blow and the silk-hatted sulked away. He did not like to be called an Irish.

Such passages involved readers with Uchimura’s preoccupations and convinced them of his candour. The only alternative to deep involvement was to put the book down. One who read through How I Became a Christian ended in agreement with its author. Biographers, as a result, have long accepted its contents as fact. Few people worthy of biography have left such persuasive accounts of their youth, but dependence on this source alone proves misleading. It is particularly unsatisfactory when it discusses Uchimura’s motivation for the trip to the United States. The search to discover what led Kanzô to America reveals much about what made the work appeal in Japanese translation and why the original did not appeal to its intended readers. At the same time, it illustrates facts about his biography.

Other sources modify the evidence given in How I Became a Christian on two important points that bear on motivation for his trip: the marriage and the conversion. According to this book, these facts seemed pivotal in his development. His inability to deal with them frankly when Uchimura later described that part of his life reflected deep ambivalence about the effect of Western culture on him. The incursion of the West – and he considered both his conversion and his marriage results of that incursion – had set him apart from his fellows. Uchimura lacked assurance that he wanted to be the man that Western influence had made him. His ambivalence gave his work the cutting edge that either attracted or repelled readers. An understanding of the way that the West’s intrusion into Japan seemed to him bound up with these two events forms the necessary prelude to an examination of the book’s effects on others.

When Uchimura referred to the period in which these two events occurred, he arranged the facts to make himself appear the helpless victim of circumstances and therefore not responsible for his actions. Yet in other portions of the same work, he showed a concern for motivation that reflected a strong sense of personal responsibility.

The two Japanese-language works referred to in the previous chapter and one other written at about the same time provide supplemental insights. They incidentally show why these two events caused Uchimura such pain. This last book is his first Bible commentary, The Book of Ruth (Rutsuki). Before Uchimura became a professional student of the Bible in 1900, his works that took the form of commentary in fact served other purposes. The Book of Ruth reads like his self-justification before the rest of the Christian community for his divorce and refusal to accede to Take’s requests for reconciliation.

Uchimura finished How I Became a Christian and the three Japaneselanguage works within twelve months. He appears at the end of that time to have felt a sense of wary catharsis like that of a patient emerging from a psychoanalytic session. In a letter to Bell, he confided: “I have written so much about my personal experiences this year ... that I have now no courage to expose more of myself, at least for some time.”

The marriage and subsequent divorce more than any other single development had caused Uchimura pain, and readers would not expect an author to dwell on such a personal matter except that in the same work he evidences concern over the other personal problems of motivation and sin. For one so troubled, the divorce seems relevant. Rather than refer to it, Uchimura interprets all his decisions from the time that he enrolls in the Agricultural College to his trip to the United States as reactions to forces outside himself. His classmates make him become a Christian. He uses the words of Hosea to indicate that he is lured away from Sapporo to Tokyo, and then he speaks of a “vacuum in my heart” that must be filled. He goes to the United States to seek such fulfillment.

In each case, the device enables Uchimura to avoid responsibility. Yet this attribution of motivation to forces outside himself changes to acute concern for his own motivation when he begins to discuss the actual trip to the United States. He starts out “to be a MAN first, and then a PATRIOT.” Once in Pennsylvania, he enters a hospital to serve as an orderly among mentally retarded children with “somewhat the same aim as that which drove Martin Luther into his Erfurth convent”: that is, to seek “refuge from ‘the wrath to come.’” The metaphor of a helpless pawn buffeted by unseen forces has here been replaced by frank concern that he attributes to a sense of sin.

Why did Uchimura feel so driven by sin? Christian confessional writings so take for granted this condition that readers tend to accept Uchimura’s experience as but one more example of a common phenomenon. Yet depth psychology indicates the important role that consciousness of sin may play in masking more specific concerns. Little in How I Became a Christian would indicate that Uchimura had particular cause for such feelings. His youthful fears lest he defile himself and his concern over conversion seem to an observer more the work of timidity than wrongdoing, but he obviously could not view them so lightly. They remained sources of considerable misgiving, later to conjoin with the divorce from Take to precipitate a profound spiritual crisis. In the absence of direct statements on this crisis, one must depend on scattered references, most of which appear in three Japanese works. They indicate that the sense of sin originated in the conflicting loyalties that Kanzô felt to his mother and to Take.

His English-language article on the Japanese personality, written while he feasted on blueberries at Gloucester, had indicated the strains that the injunction to leave one’s father and mother upon marriage occasioned in the conscience of a Japanese. After Kanzô returned to Japan, The Book of Ruth dealt at greater depth with the duty of a bride to her mother-in-law. Although most of this work simply introduced the Bible story with explanatory material, at one point Uchimura points out the book’s particular significance for Japan by calling it the Bible’s “Onna Daigaku.” In this brief reference, he recalls for Japanese readers a whole group of ethical maxims that marked Japanese society. They were intended to lessen the endemic friction between mother and daughter-in-law. These maxims agreed in their recommendation of a simple solution: the daughter-in-law should submit in the anticipation of future satisfaction. In her turn, she would become a mother-in-law.

In the light of such tradition, the late-nineteenth-century liberal Protestant egalitarian ideals for women concerned many Japanese who otherwise experienced little difficulty with Western ideals. Some who, like Uchimura, had accepted Westernization in all its forms during the 1880s found that this element in their new faith became one of those most criticized in the reaction against Westernization during the 1890s. One Japanese pastor, Tamura Naoomi (1858-1934), had written a book in Japanese during the height of Westernization that extolled the virtues of the American attitude toward women in contrast to the Japanese attitude. It had offended no one. Ten years later, when he used the same material in an English-language book entitled The Japanese Bride, his fellow Presbyterian pastors became so incensed that they expelled him from their number.

The conscientious Japanese forced to decide between his mother and his wife had little alternative. Popular tradition suggested mutual suicide through which the partners could at least escape the strain of daily conflict. To side with the mother was to honour the demands of giri, “duty.” To side with one’s wife meant that one had fallen prey to ninjô, “human sentiment.” Society looked upon one who chose ninjô as forsaking duty to parents for no better reason than selfish desire.

Uchimura found Ruth’s loyalty to her mother-in-law Naomi a biblical precedent for the traditional Japanese attitudes. His discovery must have relieved many Christians perplexed by the same problem. At the same time, it helped to defend Uchimura before the rest of the Christian community for his own intransigence toward Take. His writings and his subsequent actions in similar circumstances make one suspect that he had not thereby solved the problem for himself. In the first place, he knew that the divorce had resulted not simply from disagreement between his mother and his wife but also from Take’s apparent infidelity. The traditional ethic tolerated infidelity since it accepted occasional irregularities of this sort as natural when marriages reflected the advantages that the families concerned might expect from them more than the inclinations of the principals concerned.

But at this point, the modern, Western, and Christian element in his personality would not let Kanzô rest. He had implored Take to marry him against the wishes of his parents, yet he had not mustered courage to defend her against his mother. His Christian conversion had brought with it the responsibility to follow the dictates of his conscience. In retrospect, Uchimura could not assert that he had followed those dictates. In any case, his failure in marriage and his refusal to accept Take back had cost him the respect of his fellow Christians and driven him abroad.

A number of passages in his works indicate that the divorce occasioned the oppressive sense of sin in Kanzô because it demonstrated that he could not accept the awesome task that he had taken upon himself: responsibility to God for his nation. When unable to accept that challenge, he despaired and sought solace either as a son at his mother’s knee or as a husband consoled by his wife. When he started out to the United States “to be a MAN first,” here the word man could have – and there is reason to believe did have – the twin meanings of both “adult” and “capable male.” Yet even this idea seemed out of his reach. On the next page of How I Became a Christian, he mingles symbols of Japanese patriotism with the childish desire for protection. As the ship bearing him abroad leaves Tokyo Bay, “The yonder imperial peak [Fuji] that hangs majestically against the western sky, white-capped with eternal snow – is that not her chaste brow, the inspirer of the nation’s heart? The pine-clad hills that encircle the peak, and golden fields that in its bottom lie, is that not the bosom that suckled me, and the knee that took me up?”

It appears that when Kanzô left for the United States his mother still represented for him the symbol of protection and stood in opposition to the “man” he wished to become. His trip to America cut him off from her and forced him to seek independence. Another passage in The Book of Ruth may show how Take had earlier unwittingly contributed to his inability to side with her against his mother. There Uchimura points out how the modern woman’s concern with new hobbies and techniques unconnected with housekeeping keeps her from her functions as a housewife. “Though she knows how to play the piano, she knows not how to console her husband.” With both his mother and Take serving him in the same home, his mother may have provided more of the support that he craved.

Examples like these indicate that Uchimura, convinced that his sin resulted from his inability to harmonize the demands of his society represented by his mother and those of his new faith represented by his conscience, worked out in The Book of Ruth a solution that accorded with traditional values only. The analogy of Ruth that satisfied these values did not include any reference to the role of a living husband. Since both Ruth and her motherin-law were widows, they had only themselves to contend with, but both husbands had been part of the equation in the Uchimura home.

The book of Hosea in the Bible presented a different answer to the problem of infidelity. There the husband actively sought reconciliation with his errant wife. Uchimura, when he wrote these words, knew this passage and had been introduced to it by the man who had converted him, married him, and then became his friend, M.C. Harris. With his recommendation of Hosea, Harris probably intended thereby to counsel reconciliation with Take. But at the time of the divorce, Kanzô had seized upon the language of seduction in another part of the same passage as evidence – even though it spoke of alluring “her” – that God was leading him to America. Success at reconciliation would have invited further disagreement with his mother, and he chose, probably unconsciously, to see himself in terms of a woman rather than accept his responsibility as a man.

Although in The Book of Ruth and other writings Uchimura adopted a solution that favoured tradition and his mother, isolated passages indicate that, in the depths of his heart, he recognized how both she and he had wronged Take. In The Book of Ruth, he defends the Christian ethic as superior to the Japanese counterpart because it stresses the responsibility of the strong to show consideration toward the weak. One intuits that his mother should have been more understanding. Other passages indicate that Uchimura had come to recognize both the pain that he had inflicted on Take and the misplaced hopes with which he had entered matrimony. In Consolations of a Christian, he declares that he was abandoned by his fellow Christians, for what reason he does not say, though it appears to have been his refusal to accept Take back. At that time, “my position was just like that of a pitiable woman who has greatly praised her husband in order to remain faithful to him, her sole support; after all this she is divorced by him she loves so well over some little misunderstanding.” In Search after Peace, he suggests that a “home” (he writes the English word in Japanese syllabary) may become the solution for his sense of sin and quotes the following passage to show the forces that have brought him to this decision: “But thou the black-eyed, sweet voiced maiden take, / Forget thy griefs, thy gloomy thoughts forsake.” A few lines further along, he ends with the curt observation that one’s home is “not the place to seek peace but to give it.”

Uchimura realized that the marriage had failed partly because he had neither sufficiently understood nor properly supported his bride. His avoidance of similar conflict by living alone with his later wives rather than sharing his parents’ home demonstrated the extent of his new understanding.

About a third of a century later, Uchimura almost went into rapture in his commentary on the miracle of Christ’s healing of Simon’s mother-in-law at the beginning of his ministry. The woman had little connection with Jesus, he says, but the fact that this miracle is included right before the calming of the storm means that, “within what appears to be a small miracle, we must discover deep significance ... To seek that significance is our duty and joy.” This miracle in fact shows the importance of housework, since Jesus’ transformation of water into wine at Cana celebrated marriage. The housewife “is particularly revered before God because she does not consider herself especially worthy and because the world in general does not recognize her worth ... Cooking requires love, and sewing requires love. There is no taste in loveless cooking and no warmth in loveless garments. At the bottom of flavorless and cold society is the home with its savor and warmth, and all this comes from the housewife.” Jesus knew this and blessed the housewife’s work through his healing of this woman. “It is not a small matter, but a large one. This is why the early Christians considered this miracle so great.” And it was these very domestic chores, we conclude, that Take had neglected.

Although the divorce was the major event that forced Kanzô into his intense introspection, when he arrived in the Christian world and found that it did not fulfill his expectations, he had cause to doubt the wisdom of another and prior decision: his conversion to Christianity itself. His perception that the Americans did not accept him made him suspect that his conversion had served to set him apart from the mass of his fellows without gaining him entry into any larger community. His dedication would not let him forget his conversion and lapse into apostasy in the manner of many of his fellows. But he did indicate that his conversion had been “unfortunate.” At one time, Uchimura recalled in later life, he had written of his second conversion in America but had burned the manuscript in dejection with the English-language remonstrance to God that “Thou has deceived me.” And as Uchimura looked back on the conversion of Kanzô fifteen years earlier to record the event in How I Became a Christian, he seems to have stretched the truth enough to prick his sensitive conscience. He recalls that the upperclassmen “forced me to sign the covenant ... My name, I suppose, stood the last but one or two.”

The testimonies of others among his classmates used in Chapter 1 to describe the event in his life amend his statement in one important respect. They agree with his recollection that he led the opposition of those who did not want to sign even to the extent of an excursion to a local shrine. There, Uchimura says, “I prostrated myself upon coarse dried grass, and there burst into a prayer as sincere and genuine as any I have ever offered to my Christian God since.” Although the testimony of his classmates corroborates that he led this opposition to conversion, it does not corroborate his contention that he was “last but one or two” or that the signing of others threatened to leave him “alone [a] much detested idolator, the incorrigible worshipper of wood and stones.” His name was in fact about halfway down the list of those who signed, and he affixed his signature the day after Miyabe. He could have found considerable comradeship among those who neither signed nor later became Christians, and his diffident, qualifying “I suppose” can be seen as tacit recognition that his own ambition had played an important part in this decision.

There can be little doubt that the sense of sin when Kanzô went to the United States arose from the fear that he had willfully deserted his nation and sinned against his new God. His conversion constituted desertion from the faith of his people, and his marriage for love had flouted traditional ethics by violating their cardinal principle of filial piety. Yet Kanzô also appears to have become convinced that, once married, his intransigence in the face of Take’s desire for reconciliation constituted a sin in the light of his new faith. By the time he had finished all of these books based on his own experiences, he had worked through the problem to a solution that satisfied both the demands of his people’s culture and, to a lesser extent, his own conscience. In none of these books could Uchimura discuss directly the issues as he perceived them. But in How I Became a Christian, he dealt with the sensitive points more directly than in the others. Used in conjunction with the Japanese-language works, it demonstrates the result of Western intrusion as Uchimura interpreted it: the source of his unresolved conflict and the ground for aggression toward the West. The West and its people had hurt him in many ways, and as he attempted a frank description of Westernization on him his anguished words either inspired or annoyed.

The sting lost little of its efficacy with the passage of time. When the great Iwanami Publishing House wanted to put out a new edition of Uchimura’s works in occupied Japan shortly after 1945, it was almost refused permission by the Occupation government to include How I Became a Christian because to the eyes of censors it seemed anti-American. The second of Uchimura’s English-language works, Japan and the Japanese, reflects an increased self-confidence. Where How I Became a Christian seeks pity for the plight of the convert and by implicit extension the aggrieved Japanese in general, this work aims to give Uchimura’s own background stature in the eyes of the West. It consists of six chapters that propose the tentative thesis that past Japanese leaders resembled great European leaders: men of towering moral stature. Uchimura implies that, if these leaders had known Christianity, they would have been the equals of any figures in Western history.

His introduction deals with the land and the people of Japan. He believed that landforms influenced human behaviour. Japan’s mountains cut the land up into small units much as the European mountains cut up Europe into small segments. The similar landform resulted in individuals who resemble each other except for the difference in stature.

In his succeeding chapters, Uchimura deals with five great men; each is seen to represent a type. A short introduction to each biography indicates the significance in Japanese society of the type that the individual represents. Uesugi Yôzan is the ideal feudal ruler who brought a wasteland back into production, while Ninomiya Sontoku (Kinjirô) is the ideal feudal commoner who rose by his diligence and rectitude to a position of great responsibility for economic development.

Saigô Takamori (1827-77) represents Japan’s statesmen. He helped, in Uchimura’s opinion, to set Japan on its path toward modernity. As a person, he was humble and straightforward: a Puritan like Cromwell, capable as a leader in the War of the Restoration, but also merciful, as demonstrated when he spared Tokyo during this war in 1867-68. His only weakness was his too great concern for the opinions of his subordinates; he let them talk him into the rebellion of 1877, and this brought about his downfall. By his selfless service to the nation, he made of it a “moral product” similar to Luther’s Germany, Cromwell’s England, and Washington’s America.

Nakae Tôju (1608-48) represents all teachers of ethics. He was a samurai with scholarly inclinations who, after he finished his training, turned down a promising career to care for his mother in their country home. As a teacher, he surpassed many of his modern successors. He taught only small groups and knew each student “by his name.” His moral rectitude influenced his whole home province, so that he remained an inspiration to its people 300 years after his death.

The last man Uchimura considers is Nichiren, the great thirteenthcentury Buddhist prophet. Uchimura compares him to Luther on two counts. The first is his concern over the wrongs of the religious establishment, and the second is his adoption of a single book as the source of his faith. He depended on the Lotus Sutra (Hokkekyô), Uchimura begins, much as Luther relied on the Bible. In his A Treatise on Bringing Peace and Righteousness (Uchimura’s translation of Risshô ankoku ron), Nichiren used his religious convictions to warn national leaders that Japan would perish if they did not live an upright life. In sum, Nichiren was “a soul sincere to its very core, the honestest of men, the bravest of Japanese.” A few pages later Uchimura ends the book with the following sentence: “Nichiren minus his combativity is our ideal religious man.” As he finished his own words, he probably remembered how his attempt to introduce Nichiren into the curriculum of the school in Niigata had provoked the argument with the missionaries and his eventual resignation from the school.

Although later scholarship has produced better studies on some of the men Uchimura mentioned, the book holds an important place in the history of the interpretation of Japan to non-Japanese. For many years, it was the best source in the English language on any of the men it described. It preceded the work of Anesaki Masaharu (1873-1949) on Nichiren by twenty years, for instance, and the work of R.C. Armstrong on Ninomiya Sontoku by fifteen years.

Although both Japan and the Japanese and How I Became a Christian constitute important elements in the history of how Japan presented itself to the West, they are significant here not so much for the subjects that they address as for what they say about Uchimura and his fellow Japanese. When he set out to tell Westerners what he considered to be true facts about Japan, he assumed that, once told, the foreigner would respect the Japanese as equals. Uchimura stood as a middleman between two upright men, one of whom, he was convinced, did not respect the other. By his use of the Westerner’s language and his knowledge of the West, he hoped to elicit respect for his people.

The Japanese attempt to “explain” their country to Westerners has been a major theme in Japan’s modern development. In the 1920s and 1930s, the facts became increasingly inexplicable, and those who tried to justify them suffered greatly. The effort certainly hastened the death of Nitobe, who died in Victoria, British Columbia, after attending the 1933 conference of the International Institute of Pacific Relations in Banff, where the Japanese army’s actions in Manchuria left him greatly pressed to defend Japanese policy. By then, Japanese generals had begun to mock Japanese moderates who defended their nation’s foreign policy.

Nitobe was one of a number of writers who had become well known in the West for his works that attempted to explain Japanese culture. His Bushido still sells well and is still quoted, as is Okakura Tenshin’s Book of Tea and the works of Lafcadio Hearn, also a middleman between the two cultures who started out as a British subject. Uchimura’s writings of this sort are less well known but had appeared earlier, beginning with “The Moral Traits of the Yamato-Damashii” in 1885. Japan and the Japanese was written the same year as Hearn’s first work on Japan, five years before Bushido, and twelve years before The Book of Tea.

As early as the 1890s, numerous travel books in Western languages pictured Japan as a never-never land of little people and miniature landscapes. Even more irritating to one who saw his country as more than that, each of the major ports had an English-language newspaper with a foreign editor whose ability at cutting criticism often excelled his understanding of what he saw. In 1900, such editors presided over ten such papers.

By that time, many Japanese had learned sufficient English so that they could reply to foreigners in their own language. At least one of the major Japanese magazines started an English-language edition in 1894, and the government seems to have sponsored in 1897 the Japan Times to meet the same need. Uchimura himself was called to Tokyo in 1897 to edit an English-language column in a leading Japanese-language newspaper, and even Katayama Sen (1859-1933) planned a page in English when he started his Labour World (Rôdô sekai).

Any Japanese well enough trained to undertake the defence of his people that such responsibility implied found himself in a difficult position. He himself had very likely felt the sting of the Westerners’ assumption that as a Japanese he could not be their equal. How I Became a Christian contains a number of examples of Uchimura’s reactions to such assumptions, and his later recollections contain many more. Once, Uchimura says, a pastor in America told him to study American churches carefully so that he could develop similar ones on his return. Kanzô replied that he wanted “to build a truly independent church that can serve as a model for Americans.” The preacher then turned to his wife and said, “Did you hear what this Japanese young man said just now?” Uchimura also recalled thirty years after the fact that, in the difficult Kyoto days while he tried to establish himself as a writer, one of his Amherst classmates who visited him could not believe that he wrote original works. The friend asked what he was doing: “‘I am writing’ ... ‘What are you translating?’ ... ‘I am expressing my own thoughts.’ He could only reply, ‘Indeed!’” Uchimura would have been similarly vexed at the great German Orientalist Oskar Nachod had he known how Nachod assumed in his listing of the 1908 version of Japan and the Japanese that it was an “English translation of the Japanese original.” If these friends and experts on Japan could not understand, how much could one expect from the average reader?

While piqued by these evidences of what seemed insufficient respect, an honest doubt that Japan was worthy of greater respect made it more difficult for sensitive men like Uchimura and Nitobe to defend their nation. It is easy to forget a century later that the myths of Western innate superiority swayed even highly educated Japanese at the time. They often doubted whether they could in good conscience claim equality. In Search after Peace, Uchimura indicates that he believes the Japanese constitutionally unable to control the effects of liquor as well as Westerners. And in an early work that sketches out a number of his later themes, he says that it is “doubtful ... whether we were made to cope with the sturdy Cossacks or the sinewy Scotch Highlanders upon the field of battle.” Japanese successes in the RussoJapanese War were to allay some of the fears on this latter count, but they could not completely exorcise the nagging doubt induced by small physiques. Uchimura assumed in the introduction to Japan and the Japanese that the Mongols were an inferior race. Any claim to equality with the West among Asian nations at this time eventually had to rest on their supposed spiritual excellence. Theoretically, when and if they desired technical betterment, they could attain it. But human bodily construction could not be so easily altered; they could not, at least as adults, regulate the size of their bones.

Such depressing facts made those charged with defence of their tradition edgy. Like housewives concerned about tidying up, they had to prettify certain facts about Japan, had to feel that any Japanese who let foreigners know anything unsavoury about Japan had betrayed it. It was at least partly because he had written in English that the Japanese Presbyterian Church expelled the author of The Japanese Bride. Uchimura finished How I Became a Christian almost a year before he completed Japan and the Japanese. For some time, he could not find a publisher for the former volume. It did not appear until a year after Japan and the Japanese. Uchimura had quickly realized when he showed the manuscript to foreign friends that he might experience difficulty. He had written with the expectation of a good audience among those who liked to hear “tamed rhinoceroses” describe their conversions. But the missionaries to whom he showed the manuscript in Kyoto did not like what he said about the United States, and potential publishers there reacted similarly. When How I Became a Christian finally appeared, a Japanese house had issued it. Later a Chicago publisher of Protestant works issued an American edition.

The American edition succeeded critically but failed commercially. The president of Western Reserve University saw proofs and enthused, a “wonderful book ... [a] study which a man makes of himself in life’s crises ... What a satisfaction ... to come into close relations with a mighty mind!” At least six editors chose to review it, and they all liked it: “This book is unique; is full of quaint, strong, original ideas and expressions.” “It is real, racy, invigorating; to those having ears and hearing, a trumpet blast of encouragement.” “As a contribution to the study of comparative religion, foreign missionaries and Christian apologetics it has decided value.” “The relations of Christendom and heathendom have not produced another book, from the heathen side, so interesting and valuable as this.” Sales did not justify the hopes that such reviews engendered. The volume was reprinted neither in the United States nor in Japan. Over a century later, when Americans have relaxed a bit in the face of criticism, it sheds an engaging light on daily life, much like that of the better-known travel journals of Alexis de Tocqueville and Charles Dickens.

If the English-speaking world was not prepared for Uchimura’s message in the 1890s, Western Europe welcomed it a decade later. One of the copies of the American edition fell into the hands of Wilhelm Gundert, a German student of theology. He went to Japan to work with Uchimura after he had read How I Became a Christian; they lived close to each other for several years. Gundert translated How I Became a Christian into German and saw it through publication. Later it was reprinted. Subsequent translations appeared in Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and France, the last apparently a pirated edition. It was probably this French edition that the aged French statesman Georges Clemenceau read with the comment that he “would like to meet and talk to the author” sometime. A surprising number of senior German scholars a generation after Uchimura’s death remembered the work and its influence on them.

Japan and the Japanese never got a reading in the lands for which it was intended. It was published twice in Japan, the second time as Representative Men of Japan. For this new edition, Uchimura removed many of the asperities that had marked the original. It appeared in a German translation, probably through Gundert’s good offices. It succeeded only mildly in each country in contrast to Nitobe’s similar work Bushido, which had gone within seven years of publication into nine other languages and had been reprinted at least ten times in the English original. Okakura’s work was in its twelfth edition in 1926.

Over the years, both How I Became a Christian and Japan and the Japanese appeared in Japanese translation and as a result became available to a much larger public within Japan. Although not as influential in this form before the Second World War as either Bushido or The Book of Tea, which had also been translated, Uchimura’s works appear from chance references to be at least as well remembered today as either of the others.

Both of Uchimura’s works that were originally written in English share with Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace a sense of unresolved conflict. The similarities end there. In the two Japanese-language works, there seems to be no solution to the despair except faith in God. Hence, without it, readers might turn to the solution posed by the Naturalist writers who looked for meaning in the individual alone. In the English-language works, there is a clear target for tensions. It is the West, and for Uchimura at this time this concept referred to Great Britain and the United States. Numerous passages ridicule contemporary prejudices – particularly American prejudices – or question attitudes that Americans cherished. The story of the Brooklyn Bridge spoofs American attitudes on race. The praise for traditional Japanese government provides an opportunity to question democratic forms. What Uesugi Yôzan “accomplished in his lifetime we never shall even though we wrangle constitutionally till the end of time,” or “it is a foolishness to imagine that tyranny of any sort can make no entrance into ballot-boxes.” The conjugal felicity of Nakae Tôju allows Uchimura to caricature the West’s preoccupation with the wives of great men. He will mention Nakae’s wife, he says, since Westerners “seem to judge a man more by this relation than by any other.”

These little barbs would have hurt the members of missionary societies, those otherwise most interested in Uchimura’s life and his people. They believed that they had done much to assist the Japanese, and they would have little reason to understand in their quiet New England hamlets why the visitor whom they had welcomed ridiculed so much that they cherished. His use of pious stereotypes, such as the word heathen, for instance, would have put off other Americans who agreed with his criticism of condescension mingled with racial intolerance. Uchimura referred in later life to the poor sale of these books to support his conviction that the members of the Englishspeaking world misunderstood him. He correctly realized that few AngloSaxons understood him, but he also did little to make himself attractive to any among them except those who went out of their way to agree with him. That the six reviewers all regarded How I Became a Christian so highly reflects an ability to suffer the aggressions that emanate from assumptions of inferiority that is rare at any time and more characteristic of the twenty-firstcentury Anglo-Saxon world than its nineteenth-century counterpart.

The beginning of the second millennium found the Anglo-Saxons less assured and at the same time less defensive. The works of Gandhi had taught them how the conviction of white superiority in nineteenth-century Protestantism hurt many of the most sensitive individuals whom missionaries tried to convert. And, at the same time, the English and Americans had come to realize more that friendly criticism should be accepted. They would now find much of interest in How I Became a Christian.

Early in the twentieth century, the Germans and others who welcomed these books had broader attitudes toward mission work and hence toward mission converts. Like Uchimura, they found themselves unhappy with many aspects of the evangelical Calvinism that so dominated the missionary scene in Great Britain and the United States. Uchimura scoffed at American attitudes that also annoyed Germans. As a result, they could relax and enjoy his satire.

Japanese readers of these volumes in translation, of course, could not know the details of the motivation that made Uchimura at once subservient to and preachy toward the Anglo-Saxon world, though they could easily sense that he had suffered because of his identification with the West. Since they believed that the West had also upset their lives and threatened their nation, they welcomed the ammunition that he gave them for venting their own ire. A physician who had studied medicine in the United States later exulted that How I Became a Christian had provided him with “good material for attacks on the Americans” in his classes. Many of the scenes in this book that appeared to a Western reader to refer to Uchimura’s personal experiences would impress Japanese readers as examples of concern over race shared by many Japanese. The best examples are in the confrontation scenes when Uchimura describes his initial visits to schools where he would later study and live. He awaits nervously his first encounter with the famous man in charge. Will he be accepted? At one level, his concern is that of any young aspirant for admittance, but to Japanese it was one of their number who sought acceptance in the West. What would seem to others but an example of concern attendant upon all admission had for them the additional significance of acceptance on racial grounds. Readers also found in Uchimura expression of the concern that Western attitudes toward women caused them. The problems associated with “ladies first” (reideii fuaasuto) perturbed many twentieth-century Japanese in contemplation of the West or anticipation of trips abroad.

Most of Uchimura’s readers could not have known of the divorce, but in his interpretation of Ruth and his barbs aimed at Western attitudes they found convincing confirmation of their own view garbed in reference to the West. Finally, in the general anomic metaphors such as that of the vacuum that drew Uchimura abroad, his readers could see a reflection of their own experience with Western culture, which had robbed them of firm psychological and spiritual moorings. They also felt its forces drawing them helplessly into parlous intellectual climes.

It is not surprising, then, that these works that Uchimura wrote to justify his own position and his nation’s past before the West found their most enthusiastic readers in his own country. They took an honoured position there among his works originally written in Japanese. Although they remained for his readers a means to express the vexations that they felt against the West, once he had written them he could turn to a more positive purpose: the role that the nation of Japan and individual Japanese people were destined to play in world history. Uchimura’s next works reflect greater assurance, and a new sense of both personal and national worth replaced his earlier despair. Now the individual is seen as able to affect history. This is a kind of answer to the anomie of Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace. A sense of national purpose also replaces the insecurity before Western nations that had marked the English-language works.

The hope that one’s nation can make a positive contribution to history is both a great necessity and a great source of frustration for those in nations that consider themselves backward. When the decision has been made to modernize and the goals toward which a nation will strive have been adopted, the long years in which so many personal desires must be sacrificed to national ambition pass slowly. Every want must be sublimated in the interest of an ideal whose achievement never comes appreciably closer. The few signs of progress beckon only in the direction of a strange and unfriendly future. The easiest reaction is to glory in past greatness; even though the past can never live again, to act as if it could be revived lends a sense of easy familiarity to a difficult present.

Japan as a nation did not choose retrospection but consistently looked ahead. Of all the nations that have attempted similar forced-draft development, Japan appears to have had the best sense of what it was trying to accomplish. Stated in its most exalted terms, discussion of its place in the world concentrated on “mission” as a part of world history.

The positive role to which Uchimura first turned his mind in Kyoto was to identify such a mission for Japan. In his search, he had much precedent in history, for Japanese society had long placed great emphasis on function. The concept of an ordered role for each individual presupposes a theory of history that assigns such a role. Strict centralized control buttressed by Neo-Confucian philosophy had given the society, at least in theory, such a character. Within it, each individual had his or her own function or, to use the word most commonly employed to describe it, “portion” (shokubun) of the totality of society’s work. Another word used less frequently to describe this was “heaven’s work” (tenshoku); this was later often used to translate the Christian term expressed in English by the words calling and mission. Japanese society, therefore, concerned itself with the assignment of all individuals to their proper places, and its language had words that sounded quite like those that Christians used to describe God’s role for them.

The Western world during the nineteenth century also found itself much concerned with the problem of national roles in world society. Uchimura had become acquainted with this concern in his English-language reading. His next work borrowed techniques that Western writers had used to analyze the roles of their nations and applied the same tools to Japan. From that point, he went on to consider the responsibility of the individual Japanese in relation to this national mission. His work of theory was called Chijinron (The Earth and Man). It was directly influenced by contemporary Western thought, and an introduction to the works that he used provides the basis for discussion of his own work.

The theory of national role that influenced Uchimura originated with Karl Ritter (1779-1859), a German geographer who considered the Earth “as a unitary organism, divinely planned, created for men and conditioning human life.” Ritter had two disciples who continued his work and elaborated his theories. One was the English historian Henry Buckle (1821-62), whose “laws” of history located the most perfect development of humankind in Europe. His works enjoyed a wide reception, both in the West, where they comfortably confirmed European assumptions, and in Asia, where they either encouraged emulation of Europe or confirmed feelings of inferiority. Ritter’s other disciple was Arnold Guyot(1807-94), a Swiss who had left preparation for the ministry and studied under Ritter at the advice of his friend Louis Agassiz. Guyot emigrated to Princeton University, and in 1849 he delivered in Boston the series of twelve lectures that later became his most important work, The Earth and Man. Uchimura was to use it as a model; he even used the same title for his own work.

Guyot’s lectures discussed three topics. The first eight chapters dealt with the bases of physical geography; the next three treated the individual continents; and the last one described the march of history north and west from the Middle East, which he called Asia. In this last section, Guyot did Ritter one better by continuing the march of progress across the Atlantic to North America. He summarized his conclusions in the following paragraph:

> Asia, Europe, and North America, are the three grand stages of humanity in its march through the ages. Asia is the cradle where man passed his infancy, under the authority of law, and where he learned his dependence upon a sovereign master. Europe is the school where his youth was trained, where he waxed in strength and knowledge, grew to a man, and learned at once his liberty and his moral responsibility. America is the theater of his activity during the period of manhood; the land where he applies and practices all he has learned, brings into action all the forces he has acquired, and where he is still to learn that the entire development of his being and his own happiness, are only possible by willing obedience to the laws of his Maker.

Guyot’s thesis was well received in the United States. Several members of the audience who heard him deliver the original lectures wrote enthusiastic letters about them. The publisher included them as advertisements before the front matter when the lectures were published in English translation. Included among the writers were Guyot’s friend Agassiz, who had now become a highly respected professor at Harvard; George Tichnor, the historian and colleague of Agassiz at Harvard; and Charles Sumner, who was already interested in the problems of blacks and liked Guyot’s expression of concern that the superior nations show due respect for those “inferior in the scale of creation.” Taken together, the letters of these men constitute convincing testimony that Guyot’s words accorded well with contemporary scholarly findings and popular opinions.

At the same time, Guyot’s work addressed the lack of confidence that characterized mid-nineteenth-century United States attitudes toward its own mission. England still dominated international relations, and the small American intellectual elite required reassurance that its nation would someday play a great role in history. They must have been pleased to hear Guyot say that they shared with Great Britain the destiny of engrafting through their mastery of the seas “upon all nations the vital principle of civilized societies.” Here was a high calling, and it is likely that an Amherst professor who himself thrilled at the prospect of his nation’s destiny first introduced Kanzô to Guyot’s book.

But even though Kanzô rejoiced at the future that it painted for America, he could not have been pleased with the prospect that it held, by implication, for Japan. Guyot’s cartographer had been praised by the author for his work, yet he had omitted the island of Shikoku. The sensitive young Japanese could not have avoided the fear that his people were among the races “almost unalterably smitten with a character of inferiority.” As he thought about it, he realized that such a fear was ungrounded; his nation too had a high calling. Although Kanzô directly translated Guyot’s title for his book, he carried Guyot’s logic one step further. Progress, rather than coming to rest in North America, would continue on to Japan. There Japan’s mission would be to infuse traditional Oriental culture with the best of Christian civilization and then diffuse the resulting new and superior way of life throughout the world. Japan would act as a middleman between the East and the West.

Uchimura’s argument in his version of The Earth and Man ran as follows. The physical characteristics of the Earth determine the role in history of the people who inhabit it. As a result, humans find in geography “a prophecy formed by the hands of the creator.” On Earth, geography has shaped humankind’s development. Within the bounds that it creates, people have developed in a manner similar to that of an individual. The analogy does not hold true at one point. Humans age and die, but the race continues to develop.

Human history started in Asia and moved to the east and to the west. In the West, humans discovered that they had been made in the image of God and that satisfactory relationships with other humans came only through correct relationships with God. Since the mountains of Europe broke it up into small countries, they cut people off from each other and fostered such dependence on God. As a result, humans developed independently of each other, and this development of independence was the West’s great contribution to society.

The other tradition of human development moved eastward. In India, life was so easy that humans became enslaved by the bounty of nature. Relieved of the need to struggle for existence, they developed interest in philosophical and theological speculation. In China, because there were no high mountains to divide people, a unified culture developed. Chinese did not learn to come to each other through God alone but instead mingled with each other freely. As a result, they developed a society based on sensitivity to human relationships alone. Chinese individuals depended on each other instead of developing strength of character like that of Europeans.

Now the two streams united in Japan. As Commodore Perry persuaded the Japanese to adopt Western international relations with other nations, he acted as the middleman in the wedding between the West, the bridegroom, and the East, his bride. For centuries, Japan had absorbed and improved upon Eastern culture; now it had taken on the material aspect of Western culture and included some of the West’s spiritual achievements in its new Constitution. “The two cultures which originated to the east and to the west of the Pamir Plateau have gone in opposite directions and come together again in the Pacific Ocean. The new culture conceived of this union is about to spread out from us both to the East and to the West.” From the point of view of a Japanese “new man” such as Uchimura, this interpretation made sense. Japan’s heroes had, except for their lack of Christianity, equalled those of Christendom. The mountainous terrain of Japan gave it characteristics similar to Europe’s. Because of this terrain, its people had developed the traits necessary for world leadership. Japan’s modernization had already given the country the other attributes of a Western nation.

Although he discovered this role in the fruits of Western scholarship, Uchimura once again built on the basis of native precedent. The Japanese had traditionally concerned themselves with their place in the known world, but before Meiji they had inhabited a different world. Their concern for a place in international society at that time had led them to compare themselves to China. Uchimura had attributed to the eighteenth-century writer Hiraga Gennai (1728-79) this poetical allusion to Japan’s role as the bearer of new civilization to the continent: “Through the beams thrusting out from the morning sun Korea and China will mark the advent of Spring.” Now Japan was ready to take up the task that both its own tradition and Western “scientific” history had assigned to it.

Uchimura’s work put into words what numerous Japanese hoped for. It also provided a handy rationale for later military excesses. The publisher Iwanami first produced a paperback edition of The Earth and Man in 1942. At that time, those who directed censorship apparently so needed support for the Japanese army’s aims in Greater East Asia that they neglected Uchimura’s Christian message. This, of course, had been central to his concern.

His closing lines, in fact, indicated that only one serious obstacle stood between this vision of Japan’s future and its realization. Unless each Japanese personally assisted the nation to achieve its national ends, Japan could not assume its ordained role. Uchimura concludes, “Our duty is now, here; unless we fulfill our mission in this time and place,” Japan will be unable to fulfill its national destiny. Nineteenth-century Westerners believed that individuals learn how they can best help their nation to achieve its ends in the biographies of great leaders. Kanzô had read biographies avidly in his own search for identity, and now as a writer he turned to describe the life of Columbus in the hope that it would inspire others who wondered how to dedicate their lives to the service of history. 1892 was a good year in which to publish a biography of Columbus, for numerous ceremonies were marking the 400th anniversary of his most memorable achievement.
Uchimura begins his conclusion with an encomium to Columbus:

> Historians recognize Columbus’ discoveries as the end of the Middle Ages and the beginning of the modern period ... Religious superstition, restrained though, feudalism: all died with him. Rational religion, free thought, constitutional government: all were born with him. If there are in fact great men, then Columbus is the greatest among them.

His achievements answered the great hope of his time: “A truly great man, he gave human history a new direction, and his legacy increases with every rotation of the earth. Four hundred years after his discovery, we see how tremendous were its results ... We should learn from this giant how to become like him, broad, patient, fervent and deep.”

In both The Earth and Man and this biography, Uchimura exhorts his readers to act. He wrote history with a didactic purpose. As he believed that the lives of heroes in the past had helped to mould him, so he hoped that he might inspire other readers to similar development with descriptions of great leaders’ lives and the destinies that awaited those who set out to emulate them. Both The Earth and Man and Christopher Columbus rank among the first studies of Western history, as distinct from introductory books on the West in general, by Japanese authors. Sir George Sansom pointed out that Japan had remarkably little interest in biography at this time, yet both Uchimura and Nitobe had considerable interest in it. Uchimura produced a number of shorter biographies in addition to Christopher Columbus. Both Nitobe and he admired Carlyle’s biographies, and Nitobe became the great pioneer interpreter of Carlyle in Japan. Later Uchimura became more concerned with how to develop good people than with the academic field of history. His most ambitious historical work dealt with the Middle East. Entitled Kôkoku shidan (The Rise of Nations), it was never completed.

His concern for the development of good people led Uchimura into the specific field of individual vocational choice. The first of his works in this category he directed at the individual considering the Christian ministry, and another he addressed to the young and ambitious Western-trained people in general. As the few individuals who had any real choice about vocation finished their education, a seemingly limitless vista of possibilities opened before them. Uchimura hoped to use his own hard-won experience to help others.

The first of the two works was Dendô no seishin (The True Spirit of the Christian Ministry). Uchimura finished it in January 1894. In it, he studied six motives that might lead one into this calling: to support oneself, to achieve fame, to build the church, to serve one’s country, to serve God, and to serve one’s fellows. He accepted only the final motive as valid: young people should enter the Christian ministry only if their aim was to serve the material needs of the indigent and the spiritual needs of everyone.

The work contains many interesting insights. In the section on service to God, for instance, Uchimura points out how easily dedication to this end can become simply a means to justify one’s own desires. To know how to serve God faithfully, people would have to see him face to face. Since they cannot see God, they deceive themselves when they think that in the pursuit of their own desires they can serve God. Although it showed considerable perception, The True Spirit of the Christian Ministry did not sell well. It was written in a difficult style and would have appealed at the most to the few dedicated Japanese Christians. The relentless probing and questioning of what disturbed Uchimura would have put off many of them.

If the book sold relatively poorly because it was addressed to too narrow an audience, the other work, published as Kôsei e no saidai ibutsu (The Greatest Legacy for Succeeding Generations), seems to have been popular because it treated the same subject of vocational choice in a broader perspective. It consisted of two lectures. Uchimura delivered them at a summer conference for young men that took place in 1894 in the mountain resort of Hakone. Members of his audience made themselves at ease on the grass as Uchimura spoke, though not many of them seem to have followed his suggestion that they use this opportunity to catch up on their sleep, for he treated a subject of great interest to each of them. It was ambition, and he looked at it not from the point of view of motivation for choice, as he had in The True Spirit of the Christian Ministry, but from the perspective of the consequences of choice. What should one want to leave behind upon death?

In the first place, Uchimura began, ambition itself is not bad, and money in itself is not a bad objective. The Christian world needs wealthy men but they must learn both how to accumulate and how to use their money wisely. After money itself, another possible legacy is works. The men whom Uchimura includes among those who bequeath works are engineers and missionaries. They find their calling in the use of capital acquired by others.

A third profession is writing, with the hope that one will influence others to act for the common good. Here Uchimura includes a section that reflects growing conviction about his own role: “Literature is our tool when we fight with this world. Literature proposes that since we cannot fight at the present we fight in the future. Thus when the man of letters stands before his desk, he is like Luther at the Diet of Worms; like Paul before Agrippa; like Cromwell with sword drawn in preparation for the battle at Dunbar. He fights to reform this society, this country, to level the devils of this world.”

But each of these choices is available only to a few persons. What is possible for each of us and, at the same time, the greatest legacy to succeeding generations? “To live a brave and noble life.” If one lives this way, “the more opposition he has, the more exciting it becomes.” Perhaps because this work was originally prepared for oral presentation, it is much more informal and colloquial than Uchimura’s other books. Uchimura appealed to the gallery with humour, and, the text informs us, the gallery responded with appropriate applause and laughter.

Uchimura seems to have captured a style with particular appeal to young men. None of those whom he addressed that evening could have lived under the old regime, but many probably came from old samurai families who had taught them that the two elements most to be avoided were selfseeking and money grubbing. They would suspect any profession that seemed to emphasize either. Even among the words that they had to translate, ambition had overtones of self-seeking. Perhaps that is why Uchimura used the English original in his talks. His assurance that the desire to amass money was worthy as long as individuals channelled private ambition into a cause that would also aid the common welfare answered the second reservation of the audience members. They could satisfy, they might conclude, both their ambitions and their acquisitive instincts if at the same time they tried to serve society with a “brave and noble life.”

These works on history and vocational choice taken together show how Uchimura had now learned to use his powers of description in the service of inspiration rather than desperation. In them, he depicted the nobility of human personality as well as he had earlier described the submission required by either a resentful society or a punishing conscience. The young men of his audience felt themselves in the throes of great change; it might either crush them or make them. In his interpretation of Columbus, Uchimura had shown them what one man alone could accomplish at such a time of impending change.

Japanese have continued to enjoy The Greatest Legacy for Succeeding Generations. Its sales are second only to How I Became a Christian. This is not surprising, for the ideal of the great man still lives in Japan, as shown in part by the postwar publication of a multivolume set of Carlyle’s works.

As Uchimura wound his way down the mountains from Hakone, he may have felt a sense of deep satisfaction. In the first months of 1894, he had recovered from the intense subjectivity of the previous year. His works had prospered in a modest way and held greater promise for the future. He had put his interest in history to use and in Hakone had further perfected an effective speaking presence. His experience there actually anticipated his later career when he would work with a number of outstanding young people on subjects of interest to them as they charted their futures. Masamune Hakuchô later recalled that he had been attracted to Uchimura to discover “how [I] should live.” Although in this way Uchimura anticipated his later career at this time, he did not commit himself to it for another seven years. In the meantime, events pushed him in another direction. Within a few weeks of Uchimura’s Hakone speech, the Sino-Japanese War broke out late in July 1894. Japan attacked China over which country should control Korea. Less than a month later, one of the nation’s leading liberal journals of opinion published an English-language article by Uchimura that defended Japan’s actions against foreign detractors. The journal was Kokumin no tomo (People’s Friend), and this was the first of a series that would bring Uchimura national recognition.

Uchimura had not published in the People’s Friend until early the same summer. Its editor, Tokutomi Sohô (1863-1957), was a “new” man and a liberal. He had been one of the first students at Dôshisha in Kyoto under Niijima. Tokutomi’s People’s Friend had taken Uchimura’s side in the argument with Inoue Tetsujirô and had criticized Buddhism in a number of articles.

Although Uchimura and Tokutomi had studied together twenty years earlier in the Tokyo School of Foreign Languages, their familiarity then does not seem to have continued. The few letters from Uchimura that Tokutomi preserved deal with business and do not reflect great warmth. Even though they did not seem to be close friends, however, the People’s Friend published a dozen of Uchimura’s articles and poems before he moved to Tokyo in 1897.

These works provided the first material on which is based the opinion, widely accepted by Japanese writers, that Uchimura was a prophet. Western writers find it difficult to accept such an evaluation. One of them, Howard R. Burkle, a professor at International Christian University, concluded that the attribution is incorrect because Uchimura’s works lack the one essential prophetic ingredient: “a strong and persistent emphasis on social justice.” Japanese writers who use the term do not specify in what sense they mean it to apply to Uchimura. Apparently, they form their judgment from the tone of his prose and the way in which his various activities over a lifetime made him look like a prophet. His works in the period 1894-96 indicate both that he considered himself a prophet and that he felt a definite concern for social justice. His concern resulted from his interpretation of the significance of the Sino-Japanese War.

Japan attacked China to dispute China’s control over Korea, which had traditionally retained considerable autonomy under the spacious umbrella of Chinese suzerainty, though the Japanese had at times shown much interest in replacing the Chinese. This interest came to play an important role in domestic affairs soon after the Meiji Restoration and especially after 1876, when the nation assumed the same attitude toward Korea that the United States in the person of Commodore Perry had assumed toward Japan. The Chinese responded to the Japanese overtures with alarm and strengthened their control. By 1894, they had largely succeeded. Early that year rebellions broke out in Korea, and the Korean government appealed to China for aid to suppress them. When the Chinese sent in troops, the Japanese, acting in part on the basis of treaty agreements, sent troops also. War between China and Japan followed when neither side backed down.

Although Japan declared war on 1 August, the first engagement had taken place one week earlier, on 25 July. On that date, the Japanese opened fire on numerous Chinese ships about twenty-five miles off Inchon, the port for Seoul, on the west coast of Korea. A succession of Japanese victories led the Chinese to admit defeat in the peace conference held at Shimonoseki in April 1895. By its terms, Japan received Formosa, the contemporary name for Taiwan; the Liaotung Peninsula in Manchuria, now “Northeast China”; recognition that Korea was independent – that is, that China would no longer claim suzerainty over it; and a cash indemnity. The war lasted less than nine months. In many ways, it was the Japanese equivalent of the American confrontation with Spain three years later that John Hay would call a “splendid little war.”

The hostilities against China proved very popular in Japan, and observers of Japanese history usually consider it one of the first in a long line of Japanese aggressions that almost all Japanese supported. Ernest Young has shown that this is not entirely a correct evaluation. Relatively low-ranking army planners decided upon hostilities without the knowledge of the responsible civil officials, and some Japanese, though their numbers were few, were disillusioned when they observed the effects of victory on their fellows. Uchimura was one of these few.

His first article after hostilities began was “Justification for the Corean [sic] War,” published again twelve days later as “Justification of the Corean War.” Its tone indicates that something affected him deeply. Fragmentary references make it appear to have been a group of circumstances like this. When the Japanese started their war without the formality of a declaration, some of the members of the foreign community probably surmised, in one of their English-language newspapers, that this venture would precede more ambitious expansion. The Japanese government then appears to have responded in terms similar to Uchimura’s concept of mission: that the Japanese fought a righteous war to assist Korea and China to follow Japan’s example of modernization. Uchimura then used this interpretation of his nation’s case in an English-language article in order to answer the Westerners who seemed to suspect unduly Japan’s motives. There may have been no such provocation, but if there were not, Uchimura’s desire to “justify” his nation’s actions would indicate an ambivalence with regard to the war that required the self-assurance that such a plea could provide Uchimura. Whatever his motivation, he wrote in haste, and his work reflects a confusion rare in his writings.

He begins with a defence of righteous wars. Modern nations doubt that such can exist, he says, yet they recognize that righteous wars existed in Old Testament times. Now Japan will demonstrate that a heathen nation can even now fight a righteous war.

Uchimura then moves on to explain how the war started. Japan has borne Chinese insults over Korea long enough, and it can bear them no longer. In addition to requiting Chinese taunts, Japan has acted to help the Koreans who have suffered far too long. Korea’s “independence is in jeopardy, because the world’s most backward nation is grasping it in her benumbing coil, and savagery and inhumanity reign there when light and civilization are at its very doors. Our sacred right of neighborhood compels us to vigorous interference in her behalf.”

Uchimura then turns the tables on the foreigners. How would they have acted in the face of Chinese duplicity? Does it make a difference who started the war in the light of Chinese actions? Japan began to fight only because it had already shown more forbearance than European powers would have shown and because its closest neighbour needed its help.

Then Uchimura shifts his ground to argue in terms of the theories that he outlined in The Earth and Man. Does not history move forward when a smaller and more progressive country trounces a larger but moribund neighbour? History will record that this conflict has meant “free government, free religion, free education, and free commerce for 600,000,000 souls that live on this side of the globe ... In the war that carries such significances like these, what friends of humanity shall not wish God-speed to Japan and her cause?” Japan’s humanitarianism here resembles that of the most enlightened nations at their highest point. So glorious is the struggle that “we single-handed like to fight it to the end.”

Japan’s enthusiastic desire to assist history in its march forward, Uchimura continues, might be interpreted as self-seeking. The country’s demands at the end of the war will demonstrate that humanitarian considerations alone motivated Japan. “That nothing of material profit shall accrue to us from helping her is more than evident. The indemnity from China would never exceed our expenses from the war, seeing that her humiliation is not our aim, but her coming to consciousness of her own worth and duty, and to friendly cooperation with us in the reformation of the East.” After he finished the article, Uchimura turned to prepare Japan and the Japanese for publication; perhaps it seemed that Japan’s present action gave the work that he had been preparing about its great heroes particular significance.

No single item in Uchimura’s corpus has damaged his reputation more than this “justification.” The pacifist works that Uchimura wrote ten years later just before the Russo-Japanese War include some of the most outspoken in Japanese history. Any researcher has difficulty when attempting to reconcile these later statements against war with Uchimura’s fervent acceptance of this particular war.

The significance of the “justification” can be more easily understood if it is considered in terms of Uchimura’s own development. In the summer of 1894, Uchimura had completed over a year of feverish activity, which had resulted in seven books and two long articles. His publication of a shorter article in the People’s Friend had gained him a position equivalent to that accorded to the author of a serious article in the New Yorker. He had at last become known and had contacts.

At the same time, Uchimura felt a tremendous responsibility for his nation. His reading of history had convinced him that God acted through nations and their individuals. Japan’s Constitution and other adaptations from the West put the country in a position where it could take on the role that God intended for it; it could stand alongside the other modern nations. If in the war it did not act in a noble manner toward China and Korea, if the Western critics rightly suspected its motives, then it might forfeit its chance to stand alongside these powers, and its efforts at modernization would go for naught. Uchimura hoped that the critics were wrong. His hope and what was probably a chance government statement in its own defence encouraged him to plead Japan’s case before the foreigners.

A further complication arose from Uchimura’s implicit confusion of approval from the Western powers with the expression of God’s will. Japan could have acted as a tool in God’s scheme of history without their approval. In fact, his analogy that Japan’s action demonstrated the small progressive power in battle with entrenched conservatism might have held equally true in an attack on the West. But at this juncture in his development, his personal psychic needs required Uchimura to identify God with the actions of the nations that seemed to personify his will. Uchimura further had to make himself and Japan agreeable to these nations, for in a way that he could not understand himself he seems to have confused their approval with God’s approval. As a result, unless the West considered Japan’s actions just, Uchimura would lose his personal identity as an individual at once Christian and Japanese. He wrote, therefore, at least as much out of desperate hope as out of conviction. Government action contrary to what he had predicted could produce nothing but the incandescent anger of a man at once aggrieved and afraid.

The world now knows that in fact the government had not meant what it said to defend its attack on China. Its representatives’ demands at the peace conference in Shimonoseki and the booty that the nation garnered ridiculed Uchimura’s confidence that the war would bring “nothing of material profit” to Japan. By their actions, Uchimura indicated to Bell, they had embarrassed him both before the foreigners for whom he had originally written and before the Japanese for whom the article had been translated.

Although the government’s repudiation of his optimism threatened his own image of himself, it was about a year before his concern welled up from within him in the form of biting satire. At first, Uchimura wrote in considered tones. One article appears to be commentary on the Bible. As in the case of The Book of Ruth, this appearance deceives. The article is in fact social criticism. Uchimura called it “Nôfu Amosu no kotoba” (“The Farmer Amos”). In it, he draws an implicit parallel between the message of that Old Testament prophet to errant Israel and conditions in contemporary Japan. “The Jews of the time in Western Asia like the Japanese of the present in Eastern Asia prided themselves on their distinctive history and customs. They looked upon others as inferior, and they said, ‘We are men of God’s country; though other nations may be ruined, there is no fear that our nation will fall into danger.’ They counted up the corruption and the atrocities of their neighbors, and when evil befell them they ascribed it to heavenly vengeance.” The Jews were full of pride in their own righteousness, but Amos pointed out that if they sinned, they might also expect to be punished. He knew that his country was small and surrounded by enemies. He also knew that its freedom depended upon his people’s pureness of heart. “We repeat that Amos’s words are of the ninth century BC, and we do not know at all whether they are applicable in any way to nineteenth-century East Asia.”

Uchimura followed this gentle satire with two articles on the requisites for national greatness: “Nani yue ni daibungaku wa dezaru ya?” (“Why Do We Not Produce Great Literature?”) and “Ika ni shite daibungaku wo en ya?” (“How Can We Produce Great Literature?”).
